To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the human embryonic liver is a site of prethymic differentiation of primitive T cells.

the human fetal liver is the site of generation of T cells and the first site of T cell commitment, and that this process occurs at a stage of fetal life before the onset of T cell differentiation in the thymus.

the early human fetal liver contains a population of hematopoietic stem cells that are committed to the T lineage, and that these cells are capable of proliferating and differentiating into T cells in response to T-cell growth factors and thymic epithelium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a molecular and functional characterization of the earliest stages of human T cell differentiation, which may occur within the early embryonic liver, before the time of thymic colonization.
the molecular and functional characterization of the early human fetal liver as a site of prethymic maturation of T cell precursors.
the molecular and functional characterization of the earliest human hematopoietic precursors that are capable of T cell commitment and differentiation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the human embryonic liver contains very early hematopoietic precursors that may include prethymic CD3-TCR alpha/beta-CD45+CD7+/low CD4dull CD8-CD14+ myeloid cells.
the early embryonic liver is a site of T lymphocyte commitment and that T cell precursors can be identified in the fetal liver before thymus colonization.
the early embryonic liver is not a site for T cell development but rather a reservoir of T cell precursors which are able to migrate and to differentiate into functional T cells in the thymus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the human fetal liver is the site of T cell development before the time of thymic colonization, and that the earliest human T cell precursors are characterized by expression of the CD3-TCR gamma, delta, and epsilon invariant chains, as well as by the expression of the CD45+CD3-TCR alpha/beta+ phenotype.
the human fetal liver is a source of prethymic precursors that may differentiate in vitro into mature thymocytes.
, in the early human embryo, the liver is the site of T cell development and the thymus is the site of maturation of these cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the liver contains the earliest known T cell precursor in humans.
, at the time of colonization of the thymus, T cell precursors have already acquired the T cell-specific molecular phenotype.
the fetal liver may be the site of T cell precursors before they colonize the thymus.
